Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
  • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.
  • Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

Industry observers note that “I think it’s outrageous,” stated Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking notable.”.

Sources indicate that johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

Sources indicate that "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he mentioned on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson stated Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

According to recent reports, johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he stated.

It has been revealed that there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson noted Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

Sources indicate that A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a strategy in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

According to recent reports, senators on both sides of the aisle mentioned they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability problem, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

    Virgin Atlantic Just Axed This 11-Hour Nonstop Heathrow Route: See Map Now

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Virgin Atlantic is ending its route from London Heathrow to the ever-popular Mexican tourist destination of Cancun.
    • It will be the second time that Virgin has ceased flying to Cancun.
    • According to recent reports, covering 4,300 nautical miles (7,964 km) on a great circle basis each way, Virgin first flew between Heathrow and Cancun in October 2025.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Virgin Atlantic is ending its route from London Heathrow to the ever-popular Mexican tourist destination of Cancun. Flights from the UK's busiest airport only began in late 2025. While the seasonal service was due to pause in mid-April 2027, flights will not return in winter 2027/2028. Two weeks ago, Virgin confirmed that it'll stop Manchester-Las Vegas service.

    It will be the second time that Virgin has ceased flying to Cancun. The route originally operated from London Gatwick between June 2012 and June 2019, a year or so before the carrier pulled out of the UK's second-busiest airport as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

    According to recent reports, covering 4,300 nautical miles (7,964 km) on a great circle basis each way, Virgin first flew between Heathrow and Cancun in October 2025. It was, at the time, the first time that the UK's busiest airport had ever had flights to anywhere in Mexico except the capital, which is served by British Airways and Aeromexico.

    Sources indicate that operating on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays, Cirium Diio data reveals that Virgin originally deployed the 258-seat Boeing 787-9. The variant was used for the first season, with the final departure being on April 19, 2026. When the route returned on October 18, 2026, for the winter, the 397-seat Airbus A350-1000 was used instead. The final departure will now be on April 11, 2027.

    Heathrow To Cancun; Local Times (November 2026).

    Cancun To Heathrow; Local Times (November 2026).

    VS93: 1:00 PM-7:01 PM (11 hours and 1 minute).

    VS94: 9:20 PM-11:25 AM+1 (9 hours and 5 minutes).

    After being approached by Simple Flying, Virgin commented that:.

    “Following a review of our flying program, we’ve made the difficult decision to permanently suspend [end] our Cancun service with the final flight operating on April 11, 2027. We know this will be disappointing news for customers who were planning to book flights with us to this destination, but we’re pleased to offer numerous other options for some winter sun, including Phuket, the Maldives and South Africa.".

    Industry observers note that switching from the Dreamliner to Virgin's highest-capacity equipment meant round-trip seats for sale jumped from 1,548 a week in the first season to 2,382 in the second season. That was a considerable increase of 54% in very little time. It would, of course, be very easy to conclude that the route was doing well. After all, there would be little need to grow capacity if it wasn't, let alone substantially.

    But it's not quite that simple. It is also about how the number of seats changed in each cabin. Swapping to the much larger A350 resulted in the volume of business class seats decreasing by 48% per week, from 186 to just 96. The number in premium economy rose by 60%, from 210 to 336.

    Recent findings suggest that economy seats inevitably jumped dramatically. They rose from 1,152 a week to 1,950, up by 69%. Of course, the A350 configuration's much larger total volume played a substantial role in this. This had another major consequence: the proportion of business class capacity fell from 12% with the 787 to just 4% with the A350. It is fair to assume that traffic to Cancun was strong, but that Virgin was not happy with the yields. The higher fuel price does not help.

    The UK Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) provides a breakdown of many interesting things, including the traffic on all UK routes. Such data currently only exists until September 2026, which rules out looking at Virgin's second season. However, information exists for the first season.

    Recent findings suggest that between October 2025 and April 2026, the CAA shows that Virgin transported 35,790 passengers to/from Cancun, when the 787-9 was used. As the carrier's schedule submission to Cirium shows 40,764 round-trip seats for sale, the load factor was 87.8%. The usual caveats apply.

    It has been revealed that that was a very good result for the route's first-ever season, although fare and yield information is unavailable. It also does not indicate the extent to which the business cabin was full. However, given that the number of seats was subsequently halved, the answer seems obvious. Despite the changes to the route, Virgin is keen to use the A350 and the Heathrow slots for hopefully more prosperous endeavors.

    Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency.
    • In this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically.
    • For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it.

    In this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry.

    For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports.

    The exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome.

    In a recent development, you do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening).

    Over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through.

    Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc.

    In a recent development, global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032.

    In a recent development, if you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday.

    Recent findings suggest that generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from [email protected].

    You can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership currently expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early.

    According to recent reports, you won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire.

    There is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time.

    If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period.

    Recent findings suggest that it costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry.

    Recent findings suggest that when you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends:.

    It has been revealed that while only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process.

    According to recent reports, on November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years.

    In a recent development, note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a fresh Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned).

    Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period.

    There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry.

    Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information.

    This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more.

    You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years).

    The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to update your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler.

    Industry observers note that at some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few).

    To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay.

    When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one.

    I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days.

    Recent findings suggest that as mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal. The email came from [email protected] with the subject line “TTP Application Status Change.”.

    Experiences seem to be mixed as to whether an interview is required for renewals. For example, during my last renewal, I did need to get an interview, while during my renewal before that, I didn’t need to get an interview.

    The good news is that if you do need to be interviewed, you can typically just do so when you return from an international trip. When I did it, it took less than a minute.

    I just went through the process of renewing Global Entry, and it was pretty easy. You basically just have to confirm that all the information during your last application is still accurate, add all the countries you’ve been to since then, and pay a fee.

    According to recent reports, this time around, the application was processed in 10 days, and there was a full approval, so no interview was required. However, don’t be surprised if you do need an interview, as that happened to me during my last renewal.

    Hopefully this is useful for anyone else who has a Global Entry renewal coming up soon.

    If you’ve had to renew your Global Entry, what was your experience like?

    #158379. Latest Update: Why Most Airliners Can’t Reverse Out Of The Gate On Their Own

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1750 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Why Most Airliners Can’t Reverse Out Of The Gate On Their Own

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It is one of the more curious sights in commercial aviation: an aircraft weighing hundreds of thousands of pounds, equipped with engines capable of producing tens of thousands of pounds of thrust, sitting helplessly at an airport gate while a relatively small tractor pushes it backward.
    • According to recent reports, however, this was not always the case.
    • The reason most commercial aircraft cannot reverse out of a gate is surprisingly simple: their landing gear wheels aren't powered.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It is one of the more curious sights in commercial aviation: an aircraft weighing hundreds of thousands of pounds, equipped with engines capable of producing tens of thousands of pounds of thrust, sitting helplessly at an airport gate while a relatively small tractor pushes it backward. Despite their enormous power, most passenger aircraft cannot reverse away from the terminal and taxi towards the runway. Instead, airlines rely on specialized ground vehicles to perform one of the most routine parts of every departure.

    According to recent reports, however, this was not always the case. Some older jetliners, including the Boeing 727, Douglas DC-9, and McDonnell Douglas MD-80, could move backward using their own engines. Known as a powerback, the procedure was once used by several major airlines, including American Airlines and Northwest Airlines. So why did this capability largely disappear, and why do modern aircraft manufacturers not design their airliners to reverse independently?

    The reason most commercial aircraft cannot reverse out of a gate is surprisingly simple: their landing gear wheels aren't powered. Unlike a road vehicle, an airliner does not have a conventional transmission connecting its engines to its wheels. The landing gear supports the aircraft's weight, absorbs landing forces, and allows it to roll along the airport surface. It does not provide the propulsion needed to drive the aircraft backward.

    Recent findings suggest that according to AirHelp's explanation of aircraft reversing, an aircraft can theoretically move backward using its engines, but it requires a different approach than simply selecting reverse gear in a car. Jet engines are designed primarily to generate forward thrust, and their thrust reversers are intended to help slow an aircraft after landing. They redirect some of the engine's airflow forward, creating a force that opposes the aircraft's direction of travel. This system was used to move an aircraft backward from a parking stand.

    It has been revealed that however, a thrust reverser is not a conventional reversing mechanism. It does not change the direction in which the engine rotates, nor does it make the aircraft's wheels turn in the opposite direction. Instead, it redirects airflow to move the aircraft backward. Although this sounds simple, the engines' location, the direction of the redirected airflow, and the environment around an airport gate all determine whether the procedure is practical. This raises an interesting question: if powerbacks were possible, why did some airlines once use them routinely and then abandon the practice?

    In a recent development, powerbacks were once a recognizable feature of commercial aviation, particularly among airlines operating older aircraft with rear-mounted engines. The Boeing 727, Douglas DC-9, McDonnell Douglas MD-80 family, BAC 1-11, Fokker 100, and the large Soviet Ilyushin IL-62 were among the aircraft associated with the procedure. Their engine configurations and thrust-reverser designs made it possible to redirect exhaust in a way that allowed the aircraft to move backward from approved airport gates.

    According to recent reports, these aircraft generally used bucket-style, or clamshell, thrust reversers. When deployed, the reverser doors redirected exhaust forward and outward, allowing the engines to generate reverse thrust. With engines mounted toward the rear of the fuselage rather than underneath the wings, these aircraft offered a configuration that made powerbacks easier to manage. The procedure was particularly associated with American Airlines' extensive MD-80 fleet and Northwest Airlines' DC-9 operations.

    In a recent development, according to Boltflight's historical account of the powerback maneuver, American Airlines, Northwest Airlines, Eastern Airlines, AirTran Airways, and Alaska Airlines were among the US carriers that used the technique. However, it was not an unrestricted procedure. Airports and airlines had to approve specific parking stands, and ground personnel needed to ensure the area behind and around the aircraft was clear. The procedure also required coordination between the pilots and ground crew, including visual guidance from personnel positioned around the aircraft.

    It has been revealed that one of the most significant developments came in 2005, when Northwest Airlines discontinued powerbacks, citing fuel conservation. The decision reflected a broader change in airline operating priorities: saving the time and ground equipment associated with a conventional pushback was no longer necessarily worth the additional fuel consumption. But fuel was only one part of the problem. As commercial aircraft evolved, their engine placement introduced another, more serious complication.

    Industry observers note that the biggest difference between older powerback-capable aircraft and most modern airliners is where their engines are mounted. Aircraft such as the Airbus A320 family, Boeing 737 family, Boeing 777, and Airbus A350 use engines mounted beneath their wings. This configuration offers aerodynamic and structural advantages, but it creates significant difficulties when reverse thrust is used close to a terminal building.

    The problem is the direction and distribution of the airflow. Unlike the rear-mounted engines of aircraft such as the DC-9 and IL-62, under-wing turbofans sit relatively close to the airport surface. Their thrust reversers redirect airflow forward and outward, potentially creating powerful turbulence across the ramp. This can disturb loose debris, expose ground personnel to dangerous airflow, and send objects towards nearby aircraft, vehicles, and terminal infrastructure.

    Foreign object debris (FOD) is a major concern. Small stones, loose baggage straps, discarded materials, and other objects on the apron can become dangerous when exposed to powerful engine airflow. Debris can be blown toward nearby equipment or ingested into an engine, potentially damaging expensive components. The risk is especially non-negligible at busy airports, where several ground vehicles and aircraft may be operating in close proximity.

    Sources indicate that engine operating conditions also pose a risk. Reverse thrust is not a particularly economical engine mode, and repeated use adds operating cycles to the thrust-reverser system. Depending on the engine and operating conditions, inappropriate use of reverse thrust can also contribute to engine operating problems and increased fatigue. Meanwhile, pilots have limited visibility behind the aircraft, making it difficult to judge obstacles without assistance from ground personnel. Even if a modern airliner can technically generate reverse thrust, is there any compelling reason for an airline to accept these additional risks?

    For airlines, the financial argument against powerbacks is probably as important as the safety considerations. Starting engines and producing reverse thrust consumes fuel, while a conventional pushback can be completed using a ground vehicle without requiring the aircraft to generate significant propulsion. Powerbacks burn considerably more fuel than conventional tug-assisted pushbacks, making them an unattractive option for airlines operating large numbers of daily departures.

    In a recent development, northwest Airlines’ decision to end powerbacks was clear in 2005, when it stopped using the procedure to conserve fuel. The change was notable because Northwest still operated a large fleet of DC-9s, which were well suited to the maneuver. The airline began relying more on conventional ground equipment to move aircraft away from gates instead of using thrust reversers. American Airlines and other operators also phased out powerbacks in the mid-2000s as fuel costs, operational concerns, and the risks of reverse thrust outweighed the benefits.

    Sources indicate that additional operational costs were also worth considering. Repeated use of thrust reversers introduces additional demands on components that airlines must inspect and maintain. Powerbacks also generate considerably more noise than tug-assisted movements, potentially affecting airport noise management and nearby communities. Meanwhile, pilots cannot directly see the area behind the aircraft, so ground personnel would still be required to monitor clearances. If airlines must retain ground staff while also burning more fuel, the original advantage of eliminating the pushback vehicle becomes far less attractive. Nevertheless, an vital exception still exists: some large aircraft can still reverse under their own power.

    Although commercial passenger aircraft have largely abandoned powerbacks, the maneuver has not disappeared from aviation altogether. One notable example is the Boeing C-17 Globemaster III. Operated by several air forces, this military transport aircraft has specially designed thrust reversers that let it move backward without a conventional pushback tug. Unlike most commercial airliners, the C-17 was specifically engineered to operate from austere airfields and perform missions where ground support equipment may be limited or unavailable.

    In a recent development, the US Government Accountability Office explained this capability in its 1991 report, Military Airlift: Cost and Complexity of the C-17 Aircraft Research and Development Program. According to the report, the C-17's thrust reversers redirect both fan and core thrust, allowing the aircraft to back up on a 2% slope. Its reverser system also directs airflow upwards, helping protect ground personnel operating around the aircraft. This feature is important for military transport designed to operate in environments where conventional airport infrastructure cannot always be taken for granted.

    The C-17 reveals that reversing using engine thrust isn't inherently incompatible with large aircraft or wing-mounted engines. Instead, it depends on how the aircraft and its thrust-reverser system have been designed. Military transports have different operational requirements from passenger airliners, including the need to operate from remote locations with limited ground equipment. For commercial airlines, however, the economics and safety considerations remain very different. The question is whether future commercial aircraft could adopt alternative technologies to reduce their dependence on conventional pushback tractors.

    Recent findings suggest that the continued reliance on pushback tractors reflects commercial aviation's prioritization of predictable, controlled ground operations. A conventional tug can move an aircraft backward at relatively low speed while ground personnel monitor the wings, tail, and surrounding equipment. The pilots remain in communication with the ground crew through a headset, and the operation is coordinated with airport authorities or air traffic control. According to Fly Away Simulation's explanation of aircraft pushback, this arrangement provides precise movement while avoiding the jet blast and debris risks associated with using reverse thrust near terminal buildings.

    Modern ground equipment has also evolved considerably. Conventional towbar-equipped tractors remain widely used, but towbarless tugs can grip and lift an aircraft's nose wheels, allowing the vehicle to maneuver the aircraft without a traditional towbar. These vehicles provide a practical solution for moving large aircraft around crowded airport aprons. For airlines, investing in efficient ground-handling equipment is generally more attractive than redesigning aircraft engines and thrust-reverser systems to accommodate a procedure most major operators have already abandoned.

    Some airport layouts also eliminate the need for pushback altogether. Some remote stands and specially designed parking positions allow aircraft to taxi forward after departure clearance, provided there is a suitable route and sufficient clearance. Nevertheless, conventional nose-in terminal gates remain common, meaning that most commercial aircraft will continue to require external assistance when leaving the terminal. As long as under-wing turbofans remain the dominant configuration, the traditional pushback tractor is unlikely to disappear.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Although the holiday season can be joyous, it can be an expensive time of year, with gifts, travel and gatherings putting extra pressure on your budget.

    But with a little planning, you can make the most of your credit card rewards and benefits without overspending.

    Here are five tips to help you save money and earn rewards like a pro this holiday season.

    First, map out your holiday shopping intends and set a realistic budget for spending. Who are you shopping for? How much are you planning to spend on gifts? What other expenses should you factor into your holiday budget?

    These are all good questions to help you set expectations and prevent impulse buys that can lead to overspending.

    It has been revealed that A spreadsheet is a great way to keep track of spending and budgeting. You can simply insert your budget into a premade template or write it down on paper. If you already know what you initiative to buy, insert links to the sales pages so you know how much it will cost.

    While adjusting and finalizing your budget, remember to factor in additional costs due to extra gatherings, like larger grocery and dining expenses.

    One of the best things about rewards cards is that they often come with perks to help you save money.

    Before making your holiday purchases, check whether your credit cards offer statement credits or other benefits that could help you save money.

    For example, comes with an up to $75 quarterly statement credit (up to $300 annually) Lululemon credit that can be used at U.S. stores (excluding outlets) or online after enrollment. This is a great way to maximize purchases on clothing, yoga gear or other accessories.

    Or, if you have a frequent jet-setter in your life, you can use a credit card’s Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit to cover their application fee of up to $120.

    Industry observers note that statement credits aren't the only card benefits worth checking before you shop. For an expensive electronic device or other high-value gift, purchase protection or extended warranty coverage are other useful perks.

    It has been revealed that we talk a lot about shopping portals during this time of year. That's because skipping them is essentially leaving money on the table.

    In a recent development, by doing your online holiday shopping through a portal, you can earn bonus points or cash back at a massive number of online retailers. Most of the major U.S. airlines have shopping portals to help you earn additional miles on every eligible purchase, or you can use third-party portals such as Rakuten to earn cash back or Amex Membership Rewards or Bilt Points.

    Industry observers note that we suggest using a shopping portal aggregator like Cashback Monitor to find the best portal for each online purchase. That way, you don’t have to sift through each portal’s offers individually.

    Industry observers note that no matter where you shop, review any Amex Offers, Chase Offers or Citi Merchant Offers available on your cards. They vary by cardmember, and often stack with your card's standard rewards plus a shopping portal. Some require activation or enrollment before making a purchase.

    Related: Everything you need to know about credit card merchant offers.

    Industry observers note that we’re big fans of points and miles at The Points Guy — and for good reason. Points and miles can reduce the cost of future travel, but cash-back cards may be more useful if you want rewards to offset your holiday expenses directly.

    According to recent reports, A flat-rate cash-back card such as the (see rates and fees) is an easy way to earn rewards no matter where you shop since it offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase and another 1% cash back when you pay your bill. Redeeming those rewards as a statement credit helps reduce the size of January's bill.

    The (see rates and fees) is another great option that earns at least 1.5% back on every purchase.

    Related: Best cash-back credit cards.

    Paying your statement balance in full is generally best, but some rewards credit cards offer a 0% introductory annual percentage rate period on new purchases. That can give you time to pay for a planned expense without interest as long as you have a plan to pay it off completely before the introductory period ends.

    According to recent reports, another option is to use one of the financing options some credit card issuers offer. Amex Blueprint It® and Chase Pay Over Time after purchase may allow eligible cardmembers to divide qualifying purchases of $100 or more into fixed monthly payments, generally with a fixed monthly fee instead of interest.

    You’ll almost always save money using these programs compared to paying interest over time.

    Related: Chase Pay Over Time and My Chase Loan: Should you opt in?

    Holiday shopping doesn't have to derail your budget. By planning ahead, using the right rewards cards and taking advantage of statement credits and shopping portals, you can make your spending more rewarding without buying more than you can afford.

    The key is to prioritize your budget over earning points, miles or cash back. After all, the value of those rewards can quickly disappear if you're carrying a balance and paying interest.

    #158377. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2059 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2059 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).
    • It has been revealed that I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product.
    • In a recent development, admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

    It has been revealed that I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

    In a recent development, admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge concerns. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

    Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

    Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:.

    10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM.

    Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

    In a recent development, we arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is right now closed, so we had no lounge option there.

    In a recent development, I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

    According to recent reports, boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

    Recent findings suggest that we boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

    Sources indicate that royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

    According to recent reports, these seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

    Sources indicate that the tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

    There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

    On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

    There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

    Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

    Industry observers note that while the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

    Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

    In a recent development, so the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an glitch. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

    According to recent reports, during boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

    One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

    Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

    Sources indicate that at 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

    The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

    According to recent reports, it was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

    The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

    After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

    Sources indicate that A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

    The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

    For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

    Sources indicate that just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

    There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

    Sources indicate that the lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

    Recent findings suggest that the primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

    According to recent reports, at 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

    The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

    We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

    From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

    On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

    As we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it reveals some effort.

    It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

    It has been revealed that I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

    According to recent reports, to be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

    What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

    #158376. Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1803 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the spirit of trying out new ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.
    • I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could.
    • It has been revealed that after completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the spirit of trying out new ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

    I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

    It has been revealed that after completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉.

    Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

    On this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That mentioned, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is right now undergoing some refurbishments.

    Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

    Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

    It has been revealed that speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall K, on a previous trip. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge fresh flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

    I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

    Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

    In a recent development, if you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding….

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

    The legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My plan was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

    Recent findings suggest that of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

    I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

    No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

    Recent findings suggest that of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

    Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

    I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

    According to recent reports, I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

    In a recent development, for those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

    I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

    In a recent development, despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical matter, so I didn’t take any pictures.

    I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

    I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

    Recent findings suggest that neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

    In a recent development, air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

    It has been revealed that I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

    The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

    I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

    Recent findings suggest that as for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no problem.

    Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

    One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting new people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

    According to recent reports, if I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

    Over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

    It has been revealed that after being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

    Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

    When was the last time you flew long-haul in economy, and how was the experience?

    Why should the terminal renumbering affect security control? They're literally just changing signs, the layout stays the same. Some gates allow arrivals from safe countries to disembark airside, but others don't simply because the passenger flow is mixed with arrivals from "unsafe" countries.

    Industry observers note that looks a very nice economy product. The idea of giving the crew treats is totally bizarre to me.

    #158375. Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1248 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1248 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S.
    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    Recent findings suggest that trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he debuted a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    In a recent development, “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    In a recent development, both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    Industry observers note that “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump remarked as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Newly introduced York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump stated, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    In a recent development, other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    It has been revealed that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of problems, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer noted.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    Nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He noted it was “important” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    In a recent development, “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers noted they doubted very much would come from it.

    In a recent development, “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    According to recent reports, “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    Industry observers note that on spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to rapidly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.

    6-Hour Delay: easyJet Airbus A321neo Diverts After Engine Stall 2 Minutes Into Flight

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (698 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that edinburgh Airport (EDI) to London Gatwick Airport (LGW) is one of easyJet's top UK domestic routes, with the orange-clad budget carrier typically operating five flights a day on this Anglo-Scottish corridor.
    • It has been revealed that the aircraft involved in the incident, an Airbus A321neo with the registration G-UZMC, had taken off punctually, but the need for it to return to Edinburgh ended up delaying its passengers considerably.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that edinburgh Airport (EDI) to London Gatwick Airport (LGW) is one of easyJet's top UK domestic routes, with the orange-clad budget carrier typically operating five flights a day on this Anglo-Scottish corridor. On Thursday evening, the last of these had to return to Edinburgh shortly after takeoff in dramatic fashion following an engine shutdown, with witnesses reporting a loud bang and streaks of flame.

    It has been revealed that the aircraft involved in the incident, an Airbus A321neo with the registration G-UZMC, had taken off punctually, but the need for it to return to Edinburgh ended up delaying its passengers considerably. With the plane subsequently having to be taken out of service, easyJet had to dispatch a replacement up from London Gatwick. As such, the flight's passengers only reached England early on Friday morning.

    In a recent development, easyJet flight U2-816 is usually scheduled to leave Edinburgh at 8:45 PM, and flight tracking data demonstrates that it did so punctually on Thursday night, taking to the skies at 8:46 PM. However, having lifted off from runway 24, things took a dramatic turn when, as reported by the Aviation Safety Network citing ACARS data, the number one engine suffered a stall just two minutes after the aircraft's departure.

    easyJet Flight U2-816, November 26.

    This, the Aviation Herald notes, prompted the crew to level off the climb at an altitude of 5,000 feet and shut down the affected engine. They then entered a holding pattern, as seen above, and circled for a short while before touching back down on runway 06 at 9:29 PM. As detailed above, the flight to London normally takes 1.5 hours. easyJet spokesperson reported a "technical issue" to Simple Flying, adding:.

    "The flight landed normally and was met by emergency services in line with procedures and as a precautionary measure only. A replacement aircraft was arranged to operate the flight to London Gatwick later that evening.".

    Along with the stall, excessively high exhaust gas temperatures are also said to have been a contributing factor in the decision to shut down the engine and return to Edinburgh. Local residents in and around the Scottish capital city reported a loud bang at around the time of the incident, although, according to The Independent, Edinburgh Airport later confirmed that "there was no impact on airport operations.".

    It has been revealed that with the aircraft safely back on the ground, easyJet was able to take it out of service and assess its next steps. At the time of writing on Friday afternoon, it has yet to leave Edinburgh. However, the airline also had a plane-load of passengers requiring onward travel to London, and no spare aircraft to hand in the Scottish capital city. As such, it had to fly one up from London Gatwick later that night.

    This, the Aviation Herald notes, ended up being a 17-year-old Airbus A320-200 that bears the registration G-EZTH. It departed LGW at 12:51 AM on Friday under the ferry flight number U2-9006, reaching EDI 61 minutes later at 1:52 AM. Its turnaround took just over an hour, and U2-816 left at 2:56 AM. It touched down an hour later, representing a five-hour and 41-minute delay vs the planned 10:15 PM arrival.

    As previously noted, the aircraft involved in Thursday's incident was an Airbus A321neo that bore the registration G-UZMC. Current fleet data from ch-aviation demonstrates that this modern narrowbody twinjet is 8.16 years old, having first flown and been delivered to easyJet back in October 2018. The carrier ordered it three years prior. It is fitted with two wing-mounted LEAP-1A32 engines from CFM International.

    Sources indicate that found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

    It has been revealed that all in all, easyJet has a grand total of 22 A321neos in its fleet, with another 151 examples of the type on order. Its existing units are 3.8 years old on average, compared to a fleet-wide mean figure of 10.5 years old. As such, G-UZMC is one of the older examples, with just two A321neos having been delivered to easyJet before it. The stretched single-aisle jet has space for 235 economy passengers on board.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that there’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

    So that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

    Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:.

    I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir.

    It has been revealed that I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w.

    In a recent development, I can totally appreciate how frustrating it is when a flight is canceled, but this is actually very simple — federal regulations dictate the maximum number of hours that pilots can fly, and that’s for good reason. The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

    It has been revealed that I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”.

    I’d like to point out what makes this even worse — this was a flight out of Miami last night, and the airport had shut down due to a ground stop, because a FedEx MD-11 ran off the runway. That was an absolute pain for all passengers out of the airport, and I can assure you that American also wasn’t happy about that happening, and the impact it had on its operations.

    All would be forgiven if this traveler either just didn’t say anything further, or acknowledged “ah, I wasn’t aware of that.” Instead, he has had dozens and dozens of posts, just going on and on and on.

    He posted about how American claimed the cancelation was the airport’s fault, but insisted “it’s actually these pilots fault,” and suggested “pilots will lie to save money for their organization.”.

    @AmericanAir will cancel your flight the day before Thanksgiving and say it's the airports fault. It's actually these pilots fault. pic.twitter.com/v4t8KPSojR.

    @AmericanAir pilots will lie to save money for their organization @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/7VmOKILwCL.

Look, I’ll be the first to call out American when they fall short (and they often do!), but if you really can’t figure out why rebooking lines “wrap around the corner” on one of the busiest travel days of the year when there was an accident that shut down an airport, then you really aren’t trying very hard to understand things.

    Sources indicate that @AmericanAir why do your rebooking lines always wrap around the corner? How bad are your operations? pic.twitter.com/Id8AaTiom1.

    Why are your bathrooms such a health hazard @iflymia.

    You should hire people to clean your bathrooms@iflymia.

    He then suggested that he’ll fly Delta or United next time, because they can get you where you’re supposed to go. Yeah, sure bro, they’ll get you out of Miami Airport when it’s closed due to an accident.

    Next time I'll fly @united or @Delta because they can actually get you where you are supposed to be when you are supposed to be there…and paid for…unlike the incompetent airline @AmericanAir. I bet your life is full of incompetence.

    He’s also asking Secretary Duffy to investigate American, because “they are the most unethical and corrupt manufacturer in America.” We know the Trump administration loves to investigate corruption, I’m sure they’ll get right on that!

    Can you investigate @AmericanAir they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America.

    Sources indicate that honestly, I think American is perfectly justified in banning this guy. He’s violating the company’s policy on photographing employees, and this kind of behavior doesn’t need to be tolerated.

    It has been revealed that it sucks when things go wrong while flying, especially for travel around the holidays. But there’s a fine line between a reasonable complaint, and one that’s completely uncalled for. Posting pictures of random pilots and suggesting they’re the reason you can’t see your family for Thanksgiving is not acceptable.

    In a recent development, what’s even worse is when people explain that crew rest requirements are federally mandated, but you just remain in denial over that, and double down. American, please do everyone else a favor and ban this guy.
