    #158352. Why Austin’s Airport Is Packed While Others Feel Empty—It’s Not Just About Number Of Gates

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 36m • 📚 Deep Dive (7250 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Austin’s Airport Is Packed While Others Feel Empty—It’s Not Just About Number Of Gates

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 36 min read (7250 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~36 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that austin’s airport can be so crowded that you can barely move through the terminal.
    • According to recent reports, adam Nathan put together an interesting comparison of passengers per airport gate.
    • Industry observers note that for instance, Nathan flags that Austin reduced its gates this year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that austin’s airport can be so crowded that you can barely move through the terminal. Passengers spill out of gate areas into the corridor, where everyone else is trying to get somewhere. Then you visit another airport, walk through an almost empty concourse, and wonder why we’re spending billions building more gates there. Adam Nathan put together an interesting comparison of passengers per airport gate. Austin comes out at 637,000, Seattle at 592,000, and Washington Dulles at just 212,000. There’s a lot to learn from this, but the gates aren’t interchangeable, and neither are the conclusions you can draw from them. For instance, Nathan flags that Austin reduced its gates this year. That’s true – it closed its South Terminal with three gates – but those gates handled just 3.6% of the airport’s passengers last year. And Charlotte’s large number of regional jet gates makes average passengers per gate look much more reasonable – when outside of that E concourse, the place is a dense mess. Adam Nathan’s airport passengers-per-gate comparison Austin Closed Gates, But They Were Largely Immaterial Nathan’s slide specifically refers to the South Terminal closure, and that’s fair. Austin closed the separate Allegiant and Frontier facility on March 31, moving those airlines into the main terminal April 1. The site is needed for new taxiways and the airport’s construction program to grow. However, the airport’s 2025 passenger totals show how lightly those three gates were compared with the main terminal: 2025 traffic South Terminal Main terminal Passengers 771,354 20,895,498 Share of airport passengers 3.6% 96.4% Gates 3 gates 34 gates Annual passengers per gate 257,118 614,573 Frontier carried 553,311 passengers and Allegiant 218,043. Each South Terminal gate handled about 42% as many passengers as a main terminal gate. Moving those flights into an already crowded building wasn’t ideal, but losing three of 37 nominal gates didn’t mean losing 8% of the airport’s passenger capacity. There are actually three different construction stories here: The South Terminal’s three boarding positions went away to make room for work on the airfield. The three new gates at the west end of the main terminal were built to offset gates being taken out for expansion, including the underground connection to the new concourse. Austin is building Concourse M, a separate six-gate facility reached by bus, in addition to the new 26-gate Concourse B. Those six gates will help maintain operations during construction. West Gate Expansion So commenters suggesting “reopen the closed gates” aren’t familiar with the airport. This is space being used to build out the airport. Terminal width matters, too. Boarding lines, arriving passengers and people walking to other gates all compete for the same floor space. Austin’s master strategy identified 89,600 square feet of circulation corridors after the 2019 east expansion, compared with a modeled requirement of 125,350 square feet at 16 million annual passengers and 173,650 at 22 million (almost twice the space). Atlanta’s Concourse D project is a good contrast because it widens the building from 60 feet to 99 feet, increases the depth of gate waiting areas from 20 feet to 35 feet, and reduces the gate count from 40 to 34, with all remaining gates accommodating larger aircraft. Hold passenger traffic constant and passengers per gate rises nearly 18% simply because the denominator shrank—even as passengers get more space. An airport can have fewer gates, higher passengers per gate, and a substantially less density for a better experience walking through the terminal. Charlotte Highlights Why A Low Passenger Count Doesn’t Mean An Idle Gate Charlotte comes out at about 432,000 passengers per gate, well below Austin. If you’ve tried to get through its piers during a connecting bank, that doesn’t describe the experience very well. The airport has an enormous regional operation. It has 45 gates on Concourse E and that concourse handles more aircraft operations per gate than the others. A gate turning regional jets all day can move fewer passengers than a gate with fewer departures on larger aircraft. Charlotte’s planned expansion adds gates and improves aircraft circulation without widening the existing B and C corridors. The ends of the piers at Washington National has the same problem. Why Bigger Planes Don’t Produce The Highest Numbers Flights per gate is a more direct starting point for judging how hard an airline is using its gates. But passengers per gate adds size of aircraft, carrying more people without adding departures. So the surprising part of this comparison is how dense airports with relatively little widebody flying are. But narrowbody gates tend to turn over more frequently. Long haul aircraft often need longer turns, and their schedules are constrained by overnight flying, arrival times and connections at the other end. An international gate can sit empty for hours. And you can’t just replace every regional jet with an Airbus A321. Some routes can’t support it, some passengers value frequency, and some gates and alleyways can’t accommodate it. Upgauging also puts more people into the waiting area for each departure. Dulles Already Has Room To Grow? Washington Dulles is the most provocative comparison because it looks so lightly used while pursuing a roughly $20 billion reconstruction program. I’ve criticized the economics of that plan. First, the slide labels Dulles as having 137 jetbridge gates, excluding 16 remote stands. The airport authority’s 2025 bond documents tell a different story: 121 aircraft parking positions, including regional hardstands without boarding bridges, and excluding 16 remote hardstands. Adding those remote positions produces 137. Since that inventory Concourse E opening November 10 with 14 new gates. Its flexible layout can accommodate a large widebody in space used by two smaller narrowbodies. The number of usable gates actually depends on which planes park there. The same bond documents show 7.3 scheduled departures per gate per day at National versus 3.4 at Dulles for June 2025. The question is how much of that unused time airlines can profitably use. A quiet international concourse at one hour doesn’t establish spare gates where United needs them at another. Nor does it address the 1980s temporary midfield C/D concourse. Replacing outdated buildings, improving train access and getting passengers out of mobile lounges can be worthwhile even without a shortage of gates, although the proposed cost of the project would drive up expenses so much that Dulles could never support a low cost carrier flight again. Analyzing Additional Airports Seattle is working its gates hard. The Port of Seattle’s master plan includes a second terminal with 19 additional gates. Dallas Love Field Is Noticeably Absent This analysis set a threshold of airports with at least 25 gates, so a 20-gate airport serving around 17 million passengers per year gets excluded. That’s roughly 850,000 passengers per gate. Austin leads this sample, not the country. Congress agreed to remove and legally cap gates at the airport as a way of entrenching incumbent positions of American Airlines (limiting competition to their DFW operation) and Southwest (limiting the ability to compete at Love Field) – gates were actually destroyed, in fact six became a Lincoln dealership. Former hubs naturally have leftover capacity. Cincinnati and Pittsburgh were built to handle connecting operations that shrank. Pittsburgh has a reduced 53-gate footprint, rather than its old 75-gate layout. Detroit is lighter use than Atlanta, but that doesn’t mean flights can be re-routed to a different hub. Local demand, fares, geography and the connections already available determine whether shifting a flight makes more or less money. Similarly, San Antonio isn’t interchangeable with Austin, Ontario with Los Angeles, or San Jose with San Francisco. It’s Time To Build—But Users Have To Pay Gates are only one constraint. Runways, weather and available airspace determine how many planes can arrive and depart. Nearby airports may need the same airspace. Taxiway bottlenecks can keep a landed plane from reaching an empty gate. Security, baggage systems, customs and curbs can each run out of capacity too. Austin needs more room for people. Charlotte needs people and airplanes to move through the airport better, wider concourses (and higher ceilings!). Dulles needs to… not do the thing that was declared. And none of this explains why growing airports with millions of customers should get taxpayer money. Airports can glitch revenue bonds, with debt repaid through airline rents and charges, concessions, parking and passenger fees. The recent infrastructure law’s airport money came from the Treasury’s general fund. That’s stupid. I’ve written about using air traffic control failures to sell billions more in terminal subsidies. A new terminal doesn’t fix a failed air traffic control system. And a project justified by strong future passenger demand should be able to borrow against the revenue those passengers will generate. If the resulting airport charges would drive that traffic away, that’s a reason to reconsider the project’s cost not to ask to take moeny away from non-traveling citizens.     #158351. Tech Report: At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1952 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    Industry observers note that andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews mentioned, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” noted Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    It has been revealed that “I respect them,” he mentioned. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    In a recent development, peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Industry observers note that leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    Recent findings suggest that A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” remarked California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, released his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    According to recent reports, rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he plans to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Recent findings suggest that where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    Thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    According to recent reports, #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun rolled out his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but mentioned last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    According to recent reports, new leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    In a recent development, remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    Recent findings suggest that investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: New York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who says she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    In a recent development, west Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    Recent findings suggest that the last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Industry observers note that machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly mentioned he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    #158349. Why I’m Especially Grateful This Year

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (458 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Why I’m Especially Grateful This Year

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (458 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’m thankful for my family’s health.
    • According to recent reports, if there’s one thing I think I have to offer writing for nearly 25 years here, it’s a memory.
    • Recent findings suggest that I thought I’d take the Thanksgiving opportunity to express my thankfulness for each of you that reads my blog and interacts with me throughout the year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’m thankful for my family’s health. I’m also thankful for the way I’ve been able to grow through challenging times. The growth I’m most pleased with is as a dad.

    According to recent reports, if there’s one thing I think I have to offer writing for nearly 25 years here, it’s a memory. I remember when things have happened before, been promised before, and how they worked out. And I try to offer some of that context to the day’s developments. I remember most of the people I’ve had the good fortune to get to know since I began in miles and points, and it’s sustained me throughout the years and throughout both good times and difficult times.

    Recent findings suggest that I thought I’d take the Thanksgiving opportunity to express my thankfulness for each of you that reads my blog and interacts with me throughout the year. I’ve said this many times before but I really do consider myself one of the luckiest people, and certainly much more fortunate than I could have ever imagined.

    I’m deeply shy, which some people can find off-putting when I meet them (thinking that by not being outgoing with them I must not be interested, or somehow aloof). I’ve talked about my being a bit on the spectrum. The written form has allowed me to connect so well with many. And I’m grateful for those connections, although I don’t share nearly as much detail that’s personal many of you know me very well from my writing — certainly my opinions, my quirks, my sense of humor. This hobby has enriched my life in so many ways, including less obvious ones.

    In many ways this is still the same personal blog I first started, I write and share what is interesting to me. I usually write as though no one is reading, and I’m shocked when I get a call from an airline’s or hotel’s communications shop because a C-level executive is unhappy with something I’ve remarked. (Or when one of those C-level folks comments here or drops me a note, as happens so often too.).

    Sources indicate that now there are a whole lot more people reading the blog than when I started and I appreciate each and every one of you. Even the ones that are trying to insult me! I don’t always have as thick a skin as I should, but I try my best, because each and every reader has something to teach me or challenge me. And the positive feedback touches me deeply.

    Recent findings suggest that so thank you. Thank you. I look forward to continuing to share this journey together, and I appreciate this opportunity to reflect — and to acknowledge.

    #158347. Breaking: Your Flight Takes 10 Minutes Longer Than It Used To—And That’s A Luxury Worth Paying For

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2221 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Your Flight Takes 10 Minutes Longer Than It Used To—And That’s A Luxury Worth Paying For

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that flying takes longer than it used to – and, retirement of the Concorde notwithstanding, it’s not because planes aren’t as fast.
    • Sources indicate that by one estimate flights have gotten 8% longer.
    • Airlines are often chided for ‘schedule padding’ – claiming that flights take longer than they should.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that flying takes longer than it used to – and, retirement of the Concorde notwithstanding, it’s not because planes aren’t as fast. There are more than twice as many commercial flights as there were at the time of airline deregulation, and air traffic control hasn’t been upgraded very much. There’s congested airspace and also congested airports. We also don’t build major fresh airports – the last one was Denver, 30 years ago. (Austin’s new 1999 airport was a converted military base, and there were others like that in the 90s.) By one estimate flights have gotten 8% longer. That means a two hour flight is 10 minutes longer than it used to be. And the single biggest factor is often tagged as strategic padding of schedules. Airlines are often chided for ‘schedule padding’ – claiming that flights take longer than they should. Often, this just reflects the reality of telling customers when they can expect to arrive – although there’s greater variance than there used to be, which isn’t great for having a gate available when you land early. Airlines do not like this! Though real airfares (even including fees) are down significantly since deregulation, longer flight times are expensive for staffing, fuel and efficient use of $50 – $100 million planes. And longer travel times historically disadvantaged an airline trying to sell tickets, because it meant their flights were displayed lower on the screen that travel agents and later passengers directly saw – which translates into fewer sales. A new study finds that airlines with more “padding” in their schedules tend to charge higher fares. That sounds like passengers paying more for a slower trip. But those extra minutes can also let United hold your plane with ConnectionSaver and get you home that night, and still arrive on time. It also means fewer delays and missed connections. So that ‘premium’ is actually a more valuable product to many consumers. I’ve argued for years that schedule padding often isn’t really padding. Sometimes an airline is finally admitting how long the trip takes. Customers can proposal around an honest arrival time. There’s a new chapter by Embry-Riddle’s Jules Yimga, “The Price of Punctuality,” in The Economics of Airline Pricing. It combines 2019 flight time data with the government’s ticket price survey. It compares schedules against different percentiles of actual flight times, then examines how the resulting measures relate to fares. More padding is associated with higher fares, especially when the comparison uses the faster end of actual flight times. The relationship appears in both competitive and concentrated markets. The abstract itself allows that reliability could be a service customers value. (Interestingly, Yimga’s earlier research on schedule padding attributed higher prices primarily to higher costs rather than higher margins.) Even scheduling to the median arrival time means roughly half of trips take longer than published. It’s often better for a customer if an airline underpromises and overdelivers – or arrives ‘on time’ rather than late. Predictability matters when you’re scheduling connections or trying to arrive in time for a meeting. An airline that leaves little buffer is going to appear less reliable, so customers book earlier flights and longer layovers or even fly in the night before an key meeting. Then the buffer hasn’t disappeared, it just changes who’s scheduling it. That’s why I argued American’s investment in more realistic schedules could pay for itself. Avoiding rebooking, mishandled bags and aircraft and crews getting out of position can justify spending running an on-time schedule even before a customer chooses the airline again because the trip met expectations. American’s Dallas – Fort Worth overhaul that began in April combined longer scheduled flight times with a move from nine daily banks of flights to thirteen. Spreading flights into smaller waves reduced congestion that made some of the extra time unnecessary. One plane waiting for a gate can delay its passengers, its next departure, and other flights whose crews are stuck on board. Giving the operation room to recover can prevent that problem from cascading. In January, I covered American network planning chief Brian Znotins explaining that bookings for 40–54 minute connections at DFW were 4% below what its model predicted. Bookings for 55–84 minute connections were 8% above prediction. Customers have actually started choosing longer connections because they feel more reliable and less likely to leave them stranded. When I covered United’s media day in 2019, Greg Hart explained that 25% of its flights each day were expected to arrive ten minutes early. That gave United room to use ConnectionSaver to hold flights for connecting passengers and still arrive on time. Of course there’s such a thing as too much slack. An airline can improve its reported punctuality by moving the promised arrival later without getting anyone anywhere sooner. Excessively long connections waste customer time. And routinely beating an absurdly generous schedule doesn’t make an operation excellent. Not all padding is something customers will pay a premium for.     House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    In a recent development, “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., stated earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., said during the meeting.

    Recent findings suggest that when former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    Recent findings suggest that “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    It has been revealed that the committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    Industry observers note that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she mentioned in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack said that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack said in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., noted everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

    “We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he remarked at Thursday’s meeting.

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • As the year ends, many premium rewards cards offer statement credits that expire if not used, especially those split into biannual periods.
  • Credits often apply to hotels, dining, travel bookings or specific merchants, with some requiring a minimum stay or purchase.
  • Expiration dates vary: some reset at year-end, while others follow monthly, quarterly or anniversary schedules.
  • Planning ahead allows cardholders to maximize these credits, sometimes combining multiple periods for larger trips or purchases.
  • Credits are typically divided into first-half (January-June) and second-half (July-December) allotments, with most second-half credits expiring December 31.
  • Some credits require a minimum stay or purchase, and certain benefits will change terms in 2027, such as new minimum-stay requirements for select hotel bookings.
  • Eligibility, activation steps and exclusions (like gift cards or third-party bookings) may apply, so review benefit details closely.

    #158343. Hilton’s Cyber Week Bonus Is Worth Just $8—But You Can Stack Three Offers For 10,000 Points On A Single Night

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (793 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Hilton’s Cyber Week Bonus Is Worth Just $8—But You Can Stack Three Offers For 10,000 Points On A Single Night

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that hilton Honors will give you 2,000 bonus points per stay if you book by Tuesday, December 1.
    • The booking window opened November 24, 2026, for stays completed November 25, 2026 through April 2, 2027.
    • For stays through December 31, 2026, register for More Points to Play before checkout.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that hilton Honors will give you 2,000 bonus points per stay if you book by Tuesday, December 1. I value Hilton points at 0.4 cents apiece. That’s $8 for a night at a Hampton Inn or $8 for a week at a Conrad. Book directly with Hilton. The booking window opened November 24, 2026, for stays completed November 25, 2026 through April 2, 2027. There’s no registration required or cap. (Hat tip to Head for Points.) For stays through December 31, 2026, register for More Points to Play before checkout. It adds 1,000 points at most hotels or 3,000 at listed luxury, lifestyle, resort and all-inclusive properties. With both offers that’s 3,000 points ($12) or 5,000 ($20). Award stays qualify for the fall offer. Hilton’s Cyber Week terms aren’t explicit on this but don’t exclude them. Book a Hilton Sale rate and pay the whole bill with a U.S. Hilton American Express card and you can earn another 5,000 points once per cardholder (book by December 22, stay by April 2). Book by December 1 and check out by December 31 to combine all three offers. That’s 8,000 bonus points ($32) at most hotels. At a property on the higher bonus list, one night can earn 10,000 bonus points ($40) before you count the usual hotel and card earnings. In the U.S. and Canada, the sale rate takes up to 20% off Hilton’s best available rate and requires booking at least seven days ahead. At most Hilton and Marriott brands, $100 in eligible room charges earns 1,000 base points. That’s $4 back at Hilton against about $6 at Marriott. Back in 2010, Hilton’s Jeff Diskin explained that Hilton got too little credit for what it gave every member and so promotions let them drive business. For years Hilton offered double points almost all the time. That lifted the return at most brands from 4% to 8% before elite or card bonuses. This year two months went by between the summer offer ending August 15 and the fall one starting October 15. Hilton seems to run promotions less frequently than they used to, but promotions are core to the program’s earning proposition being competitive. It’s worth repricing refundable Hilton stays booked before November 24. The fall offer already covers existing reservations, so it’s the Cyber Week add-on that’s worth considering (I wouldn’t bother rebooking if the room rate has gone up).     Iran resolution blocked in first war powers vote since midterms

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress.
    • The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S.
    • Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, said additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    In a recent development, “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    As of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    It has been revealed that as with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    In a recent development, last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they stated they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    According to recent reports, on Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    Industry observers note that “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, mentioned at a news conference.

    Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

    It has been revealed that “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    According to recent reports, as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    According to recent reports, the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    President Trump left his Shenzhen summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin last week still dreaming of a denuclearization agreement with his great-power counterparts. But Trump’s long-held ambition to achieve the deep reductions in nuclear weaponry that Ronald Reagan secured with his Soviet counterpart Mikhail Gorbachev in the 1980s clashes with reality. Chinese and Russian officials may now be speaking the language of “strategic stability,” but Trump would be wise to recognize that these pronouncements are intended to deter him from taking the steps necessary to strengthen America’s nuclear deterrence.

    Recent findings suggest that unlike Gorbachev in the final years of the Cold War, neither Xi nor Putin presently has any appetite for meaningful arms-control negotiations. Xi acts as if his geopolitical position compares favorably with America’s. Both men are wielding their nuclear power to weaken America’s security and dissolve its alliances. Consider Putin’s nuclear threats during the war in Ukraine and Xi’s campaign of coercion in the western Pacific, which is shielded by China’s growing nuclear arsenal.

    Kyle Balzer is a resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute where he specializes in nuclear strategy and policy.

    On “For ‘Denuclearization,’ Trump Should Build Up to Build Down”.

    It has been revealed that american Airlines and Citi are working on a $695 AAdvantage Executive card for small businesses. It’s been an odd omission. The $695 United Club Business Card already earns 1.5 miles per dollar on everyday spending. Delta Air Lines has its $650 SkyMiles Reserve Business card. American’s Admirals Club card has been a consumer product.

    According to recent reports, doctor of Credit shares some card designs that Citi is surveying. One looks a lot like the consumer Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] I’ve carried for a long time. However, the other would earn: 1.5 miles and 1.5 Loyalty Points per dollar on everyday purchases. Put $100,000 of bills on one employee’s card in a qualification year and the business would earn 150,000 redeemable miles. The employee would earn 150,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum Pro, and the owner would earn 100,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum. In January I wrote about Citi testing a $150 fee for the regular business card and the idea of replacing its $99 companion certificate with a flight discount. Citi went ahead with the fee and kept the certificate. So not everything being tested happens, and I’d put the strongest prediction on a card like this coming at a $695 annual fee with Admirals Club membership, realizing that the rest are potential options under consideration (and in some cases even controls that aren’t going to make the final product). Credit: Doctor of Credit What The Lounge Membership Gets A Business Both versions give the primary cardmember Admirals Club membership with up to two guests. The personal card also admits immediate family, which matters when there are four (or more) of you. Employee cards carry no additional annual fee. The company can buy lounge access for the people who travel, at $175 total for the first three and $175 apiece after that. So that’s basically the same as the consumer card, except that the annual fee plus lounge is optional rather. American charges $1,200 to $1,400 for full membership, depending on status. And the clubs are getting better. I prefer the newer American lounges to what United and Delta are building. My home club in Austin is slated to double in size and get an outdoor terrace. Someone who wants the lounge may already have gotten the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard®. But Citi’s going to want the smaller group of customers who want major company expenses on a business account. Some Ideas Being Surveyed For The Card Both versions shared from this survey would earn 4 miles per dollar on American Airlines and 12 on eligible hotel and car bookings through American. Both come with Group 4 boarding, priority check-in and screening, Omni Champion and Avis President’s Club status, up to $100 for inflight or club purchases, and $15 in Lyft credit after three eligible rides in a month. One largely copies the personal Executive card. It earns one mile and one Loyalty Point per dollar on ordinary spending, plus 10,000 Loyalty Points at each of four balances (50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000). The other awards 1.5 Loyalty Points on every eligible dollar the cardholder spends. It drops the four milestones, along with the two $250 American Airlines Vacations credits and two $100 inKind dining credits. Instead there’s $20 a month toward Melio or Xero and half off an annual Fox One and Wall Street Journal bundle (meh). It adds Sixt to the $120 Avis and Budget credit and covers a second domestic checked bag. But its two Omni free nights interest me. On the personal Executive card you enroll and complete a qualifying stay of at least two consecutive nights booked directly with Omni to earn one free night. If this didn’t require a stay to earn that would be exceptionally valuable (I’d probably redeem them in New York or worst case if I didn’t otherwise use them, down the street at Barton Creek Resort in Austin). I like the potential add-on of rewards for $100,000 in spending, since the consumer version doesn’t really give a strong incentive to actually spend money on the card (it’s a great one to get and keep, but spending is really only incentivized by the Loyalty Points). Here they’re surveying a choice of 2,500 Loyalty Points, two Flagship Lounge passes or a $200 flight discount. American sells the passes for $150 apiece, though I’d value them as an upgrade from the Admirals Club I can already visit. It’s probably best to just take the flight discount unless the points pushed someone over a status or reward threshold. The $200 adds just 0.2% across $100,000. But for someone already at $96,000 spend it’s worthwhile for the next $4,000. Would I Keep Two $695 American Airlines Cards? I have the regular Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees], and there’s a reason to spend on it even at one mile per dollar. Through December 31, 2028, eligible purchases on an employee’s card earn a Loyalty Point for the employee and another for the primary cardmember. Both survey designs call that a promotion. On the more interesting version of the premium business card, the extra half Loyalty Point goes to the person whose name is on the card. If employees pay the bills, the owner’s rate on those purchases stays at one. An owner who earns all four personal Executive bonuses from flying could give up 40,000 Loyalty Points by replacing the personal card with that one. The regular business card’s fee goes from $99 to $150 on January 24, 2027. At $100,000 of ordinary spending, E would cost $545 more and earn 50,000 more redeemable miles. That’s 1.09 cents per extra mile before valuing Omni nights or other benefits. If the alternative is a 2% cash back card with no annual fee, though, you’re giving up $2,000 and paying $695. You’d need nearly 1.8 cents apiece from the 150,000 miles to cover both with miles alone. Status remains the reason for spending on the card. A big initial bonus could make either version worth getting for a year. I’d keep my personal Executive and look at replacing my regular business card with this new one.     Van Hollen: Senate rules changes a matter for caucus to decide

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (561 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday.
    • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan strategy Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
    • Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a strategy from Merkley and Sen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore. looks on as Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., during a press conference on Thursday. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

    Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., endorsed a bipartisan strategy Thursday to adopt new rules aimed at speeding up Senate procedures but stopped short of calling for abolishing the filibuster, laying down a marker on a key internal debate for Democrats as he positions himself to challenge Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Van Hollen joined Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., at a press conference Thursday to express his support for a strategy from Merkley and Sen. Steve Daines, R-Mont., to, among other changes, adopt a “talking filibuster,” requiring senators to continuously hold the floor if they seek to prevent a bill or nomination from moving forward.

    Van Hollen went further to say that while his personal view is that the filibuster itself is “anti-democratic,” changes beyond what Merkley and Daines are proposing are a matter for further discussion.

    It has been revealed that “I’m in favor of filibuster reform,” Van Hollen remarked. “How and when we do that is a matter for the caucus to decide.”.

    The filibuster, a Senate tactic that effectively requires a 60-vote threshold to advance most legislation, has long been the subject of calls for change or outright abolition from members of both parties.

    Other changes Merkley and Daines unveiled in October include eliminating cloture requirements for nominations and amendments, reducing post-cloture time for legislation, and introducing a newly introduced suspension process modeled after the House rules to allow bills with broad support to move rapidly.

    Merkley actually held two separate press conferences Thursday on his filibuster proposal, one with his Montana Republican co-sponsor and then later with Van Hollen, whose bid to become majority leader he has endorsed.

    At the earlier appearance, Daines mentioned that he thought the changes, if adopted, would “truly be a cultural change for the Senate” and lead to greater bipartisanship.

    “We believe these reforms are appropriate no matter who is in the majority, no matter what the election outcomes were,” Daines remarked.

    Daines also reiterated his view that implementing any rules changes would require 67 votes from the full chamber.

    But Democrats have been debating whether to use their new majority in 2027 to change the rules on the first day of the session with 51 votes, or to eventually employ the so-called “nuclear option,” a series of procedural moves leading to a simple majority vote.

    Industry observers note that democrats used that tool in 2013 to lower the voting threshold for advancing some presidential nominations with a simple majority, rather than 60 votes. A Republican majority followed in 2017 by extending that change to include Supreme Court nominations, and again in 2019 to reduce the number of hours between a cloture and final confirmation vote.

    A spokesperson for Schumer declined to comment on Van Hollen’s endorsement of the Merkley-Daines proposal.

    Schumer has remarked he remains confident in his bid to remain party leader.

    Van Hollen reiterated Thursday that his “momentum is growing,” after several senators-elect have thrown their support behind the Maryland Democrat.

    “I think people recognize that if we're going to deliver on the significant things that the American voters stood up for and voted for, you can't just go back to business as usual and status quo,” Van Hollen noted.

    Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen (D.), who is challenging Chuck Schumer for the position of Senate majority leader, is adopting this playbook. Van Hollen, who alleged in a recent Latest York Times op-ed that Israelis have “increasingly undermined American interests and values,” has become one of the foremost critics of the Jewish state in Congress.     📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Air travelers returning home from Thanksgiving can breathe a sigh of relief.

    Flight schedules were close to normal on Friday after a series of storms snarled flights on both coasts during the run-up to Thanksgiving.

    And Mother Nature appeared not to have any more major curveballs to throw at travelers between now and Sunday, normally one of the busiest air travel periods of the year as holiday-goers return home.

    Recent findings suggest that that came after more than 460 flights were canceled on Thursday, according to data from FlightAware. The bad weather complicated the plans of tens of thousands of travelers with flights on Thanksgiving Day. East Coast airports serving the metro areas of Fresh York City, Washington, D.C., Boston, Philadelphia and Baltimore were the hardest hit, but disruptions rippled across airports in Florida, the Midwest and the West Coast.

    The main culprit: A Thanksgiving Day coastal storm on the East Coast that was strong enough to cause the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in Midtown Manhattan.

    This week's flight problems came after a chaotic few weeks for air travel in the U.S., which featured a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 — and then tech outages at two of the largest U.S. carriers.

    Now, Mother Nature has interfered with holiday travelers' plans.

    “The timing couldn’t be worse,” Fox Weather meteorologist Bob Van Dillen had told TPG entering the Thanksgiving rush.

    We've often seen how significant East Coast storms can snarl air traffic. With so many key airline hubs, a major weather system can cause cascading flight woes across the country.

    Major airlines rolled out weather-related rebooking policies for airports facing poor conditions:.

    While Thursday could be a messy weather day, Thanksgiving Day itself typically brings much smaller crowds to airports.

    According to preliminary data from the Transportation Security Administration, Thursday was the single quietest day at U.S. airports in nearly five years.

    The forecast looks favorable through Sunday as travelers return from the holiday. The Sunday after Thanksgiving is typically the single busiest day of the year to fly.

    Sources indicate that last year, the post-Thanksgiving rush set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports for passenger traffic.

    According to recent reports, entering the holiday rush, the TSA had projected more than 3 million passengers could fly on Nov. 29. That would be the first time U.S. passenger traffic would eclipse that mark in 2026.

    Here are some things you should do if you've been affected by bad weather this holiday week, or strategy to fly on the upcoming busy Sunday.

    Keep an eye out for airline travel advisories (see above) that could allow you more flexibility to change your itinerary.

    In a recent development, take a close look at the forecast in every city you’ll be in — including wherever you might be connecting. That should give you a better sense of when the problem periods could be.

    Just keep in mind: As more and more cities are affected by bad weather, disruptions could cascade across airlines’ networks.

    Sources indicate that have your airline’s app downloaded, familiarize yourself with it, and opt in to all push notifications. Use it to:.

    According to recent reports, want to know how the TPG team deals with travel trouble? Check out some of our top strategies.

    When it comes to bad weather, airlines typically will not foot the bill for unexpected hotel stays, meals and ride-hailing services.

    However, if you booked your flight with a credit card that has built-in travel insurance, you may be able to file a claim and get some reimbursement.

    Also, if you previously purchased a travel insurance strategy for this trip — or have an existing annual plan — that may cover you, too.

    Just be sure to keep all your receipts.

    #158332. SEC Proposes Reforms to Shareholder Democracy

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (228 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    SEC Proposes Reforms to Shareholder Democracy

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (228 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, every year, corporate shareholders have several hundred proposals to vote on at corporate annual meetings or, more often, via their proxy ballots.
    • Unlike many federal rule changes, which often include relatively minor tweaks to the existing bureaucracy, the SEC’s current proposal would repeal a major regulation known as Rule 14a-8 that’s been on the books for decades.
    • Richard Morrison is the host of the Free the Economy podcast and a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, every year, corporate shareholders have several hundred proposals to vote on at corporate annual meetings or, more often, via their proxy ballots. Those proposals have become more controversial and divisive over time. The last several years of battles over “woke capitalism” and its inevitable backlash were largely fought through the shareholder resolution process. Now the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is about to rewrite the rules for what makes it onto those shareholder ballots, and that could mean a reset for how politics impacts corporate America — and vice versa.

    Unlike many federal rule changes, which often include relatively minor tweaks to the existing bureaucracy, the SEC’s current proposal would repeal a major regulation known as Rule 14a-8 that’s been on the books for decades. Originally implemented in 1942 and amended multiple times since, the rule gave the SEC the power to referee which ideas corporate boards need to put up for a vote and which ones they can safely ignore. But the SEC is now proposing to repeal the rule entirely, leaving those decisions up to state governments and individual companies.

    Richard Morrison is the host of the Free the Economy podcast and a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    Alec Mena is a research fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    On “SEC Proposes Reforms to Shareholder Democracy”.

    Latest Update: GAO chief nominee triggers partisan clash at Senate hearing

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday.
    • Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.
    • “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Eric Ueland, nominee to be comptroller general, sits at the witness table for his confirmation hearing with the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    Eric Ueland, President Donald Trump’s pick for comptroller general, promised to be independent and impartial if confirmed, amid criticism from Democrats and outside groups, during a confirmation hearing Thursday.

    “I’m not here as a plant, a stooge, a lackey for anybody,” he told Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., after Democrats on the panel accused him of being a “rubber stamp” for the administration.

    Democrats have criticized Ueland, a longtime GOP Senate aide and administration official during both Trump terms, saying he is too politically biased to lead the nonpartisan watchdog agency which conducts investigations and audits for Congress. They also stated Republicans ignored a law that Democrats say requires the convening of a special legislative commission to make recommendations for the post.

    Ueland said if the Senate confirms him to lead the Government Accountability Office, “We can at the end of the day ... see a GAO which is more effective, which provides better information for Congress in a quicker way so Congress is able to take policy actions and drive change itself at this end of Pennsylvania Avenue.”.

    At the root of the partisan clash is a suspicion by Democrats that Trump is trying to install a puppet to lead an agency that has fought the administration repeatedly over the power of the purse and other matters.

    Democrats blasted Paul for rushing the hearing, which included a dozen other nominees for administration and judicial posts.

    “It’s so apparent that this is a box-checking exercise,” mentioned Sen. Gary Peters of Michigan, the ranking Democrat on the panel. “This committee is not doing due diligence, despite some of our members’ best efforts, because the chairman has chosen not to carry out his responsibility to provide advice and consent on nominations.”.

    Democrats mentioned Paul did not allow Peters to make an opening statement at the hearing and restricted the amount of time given to senators to ask questions. A GOP aide disputed this, noting that Paul did not give an opening statement himself, Peters arrived late and all senators were given five minutes to ask questions.

    Ueland has served as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget under Russ Vought, the OMB director. Trump nominated Ueland to head the GAO, a legislative branch agency, Monday.

    Democrats noted that the GAO has concluded multiple times that the administration violated the law by "impounding," or refusing to spend, appropriated funds. OMB has argued that the GAO misread the law and that it does not have any authority over the executive branch.

    Peters told Ueland that the GAO had issued 12 reports accusing the administration of violating the law, and he asked if Ueland agreed.

    Ueland did not give a direct response.

    “First, many of those items indicated by those reports, I have not participated in,” he said. Ueland said he had not reviewed the reports that Peters provided to him earlier, and that he would not offer an opinion on them.

    He also said it was critical that he “not prejudge or come to this committee with informed conclusions about what it is that GAO has rendered as advice to Congress.” Ueland said he has a “clear commitment to follow the process.”.

    Peters stated when Ueland appeared before the committee last year after being nominated for the OMB post, he voiced support for the presidential authority of impoundment.

    “We’re going to expect you to continue to basically ignore Congress,” Peters said. “You’re going to be a rubber stamp for the administration.”.

    “That’s not so,” Ueland replied.

    Ueland noted his experience as deputy overseeing the management side of OMB would be a “value add to GAO.” He cited his work “examining how the government actually functions, how it is organized, how it can be better optimized to deliver results.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, asked Ueland how he would grade GAO’s work to date.

    Ueland noted he would give it a “medium grade over time.”.

    For example, he noted GAO has 38 government operations on a “high-risk list … some of which have been on there for 36 years.”.

    By contrast, Ueland referred to his work at OMB, where he said “you have seen a very swift and aggressive effort by this administration in this term to set up systems and processes to ensure that we are not sending money out the door that we shouldn’t.”.

    Paul asked Ueland what he would do if administration officials told him they did not like a GAO investigation or conclusion.

    Ueland said he would “fully follow through on charges from Congress and in the event of obstacles figure out ways to proceed to try to elicit information.” He said when he was a young staffer in the Senate, when there were disagreements between the legislative and executive branches, GAO and the administration had conversations “to see if there were appropriate paths forward.”.

    Responding to another question from Paul as to whether he would ignore a potential request from the White House to stop an investigation, Ueland noted, “To be clear, yes.”.

    Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., who is seeking to be the ranking Republican on the committee in the next Congress, said he was satisfied that Republicans followed the letter of the law requiring a commission to make recommendations to the president for comptroller general. He added that he was not “completely sure they have followed the entire spirit of the law.”.

    In a recent development, “For me, personally, Mr. Ueland is a great candidate in this role for GAO,” Lankford said.

    Paul sent three recommendations for comptroller general, including Ueland, to the White House last week from the six Republican members of a 10-member bipartisan, bicameral commission. But he never convened the body to seek applications from and interview candidates for the post.

    In a recent development, and he gave the four Democrats on the commission less than 24 hours’ notice last week to offer their recommendations. Democrats charged that Paul subverted the process, and they did not offer recommendations.

    In a separate interview Wednesday, the president of the union that represents GAO employees decried the decision not to follow the commission process that characterized past comptroller general nominations.

    “We see that bipartisan process as extremely vital to preserving and keeping the trust that GAO has with the entire Congress,” stated Benjamin Emmel, president of Local 1921 of the International Federation of Professionals and Technical Engineers.

    Emmel, a senior analyst at GAO, remarked by sidestepping that procedure, “there is a cloud that hangs above any nominee where one party dominates that process.”.

    Industry observers note that he remarked GAO’s credibility depends on members of both parties trusting that the organization is “nonpartisan, objective, independent and fair. If we lose that ability, we become less useful.”.

    The union is not advocating for or against Ueland or any nominee for the office. The Homeland Security panel is not expected to vote on the nominations until after Thanksgiving.
