    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Sweeping permitting overhaul passes Senate, on to House

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1492 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that from left, Sens.
    • The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.
    • It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that from left, Sens. Mike Lee, R-Utah., Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the measure in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would overhaul the federal permitting system for electric power lines, power lines wind and solar farms, hard rock mining and oil drilling projects and more.

    It's the culmination of a yearslong effort intended to address industry concerns that it is too difficult to build any major infrastructure project in the United States. Supporters overcame opposition from more than half the Democratic Caucus, which will be a factor when the bill moves to the House after the Thanksgiving recess.

    The bill passed on a 62-33 vote, with 31 Democrats joining two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, in opposition.

    Shortly after the post-cloture time expired late Thursday, the Senate voted on passage of the legislation, including a substitute amendment consisting of revised text of the original permitting bill that the bipartisan authors unveiled before the midterm elections.

    However, the chamber did not consider any additional amendments to the bill, as initially planned by the sponsors, including Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., panel ranking member Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Mike Lee, R-Utah, and panel ranking member Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.

    The bill includes changes to how reviews are conducted and permits are issued under the National Environmental Policy Act, National Historic Preservation Act, Endangered Species Act, Federal Power Act and Clean Water Act.

    It includes provisions intended to ensure electricity ratepayers are not saddled with the costs of bringing power to data centers, and would give the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission new authority over interstate transmission lines.

    It also would provide legal recourse when administrations discriminate against certain forms of energy or seek to revisit permits on ideological grounds. That's intended in part to address the Trump administration’s actions to delay or block solar and wind energy projects.

    In a recent development, democrats walked away from negotiations last year due to Trump administration actions to block offshore wind construction. However they ultimately said they received sufficient assurances that the administration would let stalled wind and solar projects move forward.

    The "big four" senators on the permitting bill solicited feedback and changes sought by various lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, and were open to votes on additional amendments — so long as they didn't undo the measure's core tenets.

    "This bill has threaded a needle the likes of which this chamber has not seen in a while, and we’ve got to take advantage of this opportunity," Capito said before passage.

    Ultimately, Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden would not consent to a time agreement allowing consideration of a finite number of amendments because Republicans wouldn't allow up-or-down votes at a simple-majority threshold on some of theirs. Merkley then objected to a unanimous consent request to consider amendments on the floor.

    Recent findings suggest that wyden was pushing for a vote on an amendment that would prohibit construction of data centers on federal public lands. Merkley was pushing for amendments that included barring data centers from benefiting from “project certainty” protections against future presidents revoking their permits, and limiting presidential power to impose tariffs on clean energy project components, like wind turbines.

    According to recent reports, the Senate had already adopted the substitute amendment introduced by the bill’s sponsors during a procedural vote on Wednesday. But the lack of a unanimous consent agreement to take up more amendments meant that an additional manager's package of changes to the substitute fell by the wayside.

    That amendment would have narrowed the instances where exemptions from National Historic Preservation Act reviews would be allowed, increased the annual authorization for the Historic Preservation Fund by 50 percent, and addressed concerns about the use of eminent domain when permitting transmission projects raised by Hawley and Rounds.

    The sponsors introduced an updated version of their manager’s amendment Thursday afternoon that would refine exemptions from the ratepayer projection provisions so that artificial intelligence "hyperscalers" can't escape through a loophole.

    The original manager's amendment sought to exempt internet and telecommunications providers' facilities, but the language was broad enough that cloud storage and other "information services" exclusions could potentially benefit data centers.

    None of those changes made it into the bill as a result of the stalemate over amendments, and Merkley objected on the floor to incorporating just the manager's package.

    It has been revealed that the bill has been endorsed by a wide range of industry groups, who argue that the current federal permitting regime makes it too difficult to finance, blueprint and construct projects domestically. This includes the American Petroleum Institute, the American Clean Power Association, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers.

    The White House expressed its support for the bill in a statement of administration policy this month.

    The bill now moves on to the House, where it seemingly has the votes to pass.

    According to recent reports, speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., remarked last week that the bill can pass in that chamber, while a number of Democrats including the centrist Blue Dog Coalition and Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., co-chair of the bipartisan Climate Solutions Caucus, and Nikki Budzinski, D-Ill., have expressed support.

    Budzinski was elected chair of the 112-member Fresh Democrat Coalition last week for the next Congress, and that group issued a statement speaking favorably of permitting while stopping short of endorsing the bill as right now drafted.

    However, attendance on the House GOP side after Thanksgiving could be an matter: more than 30 lawmakers regularly skipped votes this week, the majority of them Republicans.

    And many Democrats have called on Heinrich and Whitehouse to punt consideration of the bill to the latest Congress, when their party will have large majorities in both chambers.

    Merkley, who is in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, and House Natural Resources ranking member Jared Huffman, D-Calif. — the expected chairman of that panel — both said the bill included too many provisions Democrats opposed in order to garner Republican support.

    Recent findings suggest that some of the nation’s largest environmental groups including the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council oppose the bill. A coalition of 17 Democratic states also expressed their opposition. And some Native American tribes and organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, also expressed their opposition.

    "I’m hoping to have a full opportunity to address the many legitimate concerns that stakeholders have raised with this bill," Merkley remarked before the vote Thursday night.

    According to recent reports, but Heinrich and Whitehouse resisted calls to delay the bill, arguing that President Donald Trump is in office for two more years and that any bill needs his support to be signed into law. They added that they will be able to address environmental problems under their majority, and that this bill would represent the “floor” of their ambitions.

    While Republicans have called for changes to the federal permitting system for decades, the effort gained steam with Democrats after the passage of their 2022 reconciliation law, which they dubbed the Inflation Reduction Act, or IRA.

    As part of the deal to get then-Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chairman Joe Manchin III, D-W.Va., on board with the IRA, the Biden administration agreed to support a bill overhauling the federal permitting system. Manchin introduced a bill that included changes to NEPA and transmission permitting, and would approve all remaining permits needed for the Mountain Valley Pipeline in his home state.

    However, his effort ultimately fell short on a 47-47 procedural vote to attach the bill to that year’s defense authorization measure.

    In the 118th Congress Manchin tried again, and in 2024 he and then-Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso, R-Wyo., introduced what Manchin called a “perfectly crafted balance.” The committee approved that bill in July 2024, but it was never voted on by the full Senate.

    Capito, Whitehouse, Lee and Heinrich made a collective commitment to address permitting overhaul when they stepped into their current roles in January 2025, and spent nearly 21 months working on the legislation.

    Since Manchin’s first bill, the political calculus changed.

    Recent findings suggest that after decades of stagnant energy demand, electricity prices began rising in part due to the expansion of data centers. Consumers also became increasingly frustrated with their local utilities over affordability concerns, which in turn spurred more lawmakers across the country, including on Capitol Hill, to critically examine their practices.

    It has been revealed that lee also pushed for language streamlining NHPA reviews, which had not been a focus of earlier permitting discussion. He's argued that the law has expanded beyond its originally intended scope and become a major barrier to infrastructure projects in Western states like Utah.

    Recent findings suggest that norse’s efforts to diversify beyond low-cost, long-haul flying ultimately proved insufficient to keep its planes in the air. The focus now shifts to what, if anything, can be salvaged from the business.

    Norse Atlantic Airways has canceled all flights and discontinued ticket sales after its Norwegian operating subsidiary noted it is filing for bankruptcy.

    The collapse comes a day after the low-cost, long-haul carrier suspended flights and two days after it described its financial situation as “critical.”.

    In a stock exchange filing on Friday, Norse confirmed that the board of its Norwegian operating subsidiary, Norse Atlantic Airways AS, had concluded there was no longer a basis for continued operations. The board resolved to file a bankruptcy petition with a local court, which will appoint a trustee to oversee the process.

    The filing does not extend to the listed parent organization, Norse Atlantic ASA, or its UK operating subsidiary. Norse mentioned efforts are continuing to find a solution that would allow the remaining parts of the business to continue operating.

    However, flights operated by both the Norwegian and British airlines have been cance.

    • Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

    It has been revealed that I’m thankful for one little moment on Monday this week, around 5:05 p.m. The dark of night was falling over most of the sky, except for a brilliant ring of purple just over the tree line to one side of us. We pulled the minivan into the parking lot of the karate studio, and my eight-year-old son hopped out of the car, grabbing my hand as we passed through the parking lot. I gave it a little squeeze, and he squeezed it back. Maybe just a few more years of that. He earned his first stripes on his white belt that night.

    It has been revealed that I’m thankful for my older son’s soccer coach, who has known him for over three years now, moving my boy up from an in-house program, to a Sunday league, and this fall to the EDP (Elite Development Program), where this cheap-as-chips town team plays (and usually defeats) all the expensive “academy teams” in our area. My son was not, at first, a natural athlete — in fact, he was quite clumsy. But he had this enormous engine in him to run, and over the years developed patience for himself to work. His coach recognized him, coached his oversensitivity out of him, made him work — and enjoy working — harder than he ever would have done just by himself.

    Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review Online.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Photo Credit: Leonardo Hotel, Brighton, UK © José by Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro.
    • Leonardo's UK hotels are making money from guests, but not enough to cover the rent.
    • Rising wages and payroll taxes are squeezing Leonardo Hotels' UK business, but the bigger problem is the rent on its hotels, according to accounts filed with Companies House, the UK organization register.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Photo Credit: Leonardo Hotel, Brighton, UK © José by Luiz Bernardes Ribeiro. Wikimedia Commons.

    Leonardo's UK hotels are making money from guests, but not enough to cover the rent. With costs rising and more rooms coming onto the market, the lease-heavy model that let hotel groups expand fast in the UK is starting to look like a liability.

    Rising wages and payroll taxes are squeezing Leonardo Hotels' UK business, but the bigger problem is the rent on its hotels, according to accounts filed with Companies House, the UK organization register.

    It has been revealed that on paper, the drop is steep. The hotel chain swung to a £55.6 million ($74 million) pre-tax loss in 2025 from a £50.1 million ($67 million) profit. But the 2024 profit included an £89.8 million ($119 million) one-off gain from revaluing its leases. Without it, 2024 would have shown a loss of about £40 million ($53 million), so the loss widened by about £16 million ($21 million) rather than appearing from nowhere.

    The filing demonstrates revenue at Leonardo Hotel Management (UK) Ltd was steady, rising 1.3% to £350.1 million ($466 million), with no newly introduced hotels opened. Gross profit fell 12% to £37.6 million ($50 million), and the gross margin slipped to 10.7% from 12.4%. Staff costs rose 6% to £102.5 million ($136 million), and employer social security costs rose 34%.

    According to recent reports, on the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most notable midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”.

    “When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump stated, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”.

    Sources indicate that “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump mentioned midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”.

    The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the Newly introduced York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

    Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the Upcoming York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how substantial a role early votes will play in the outcome.

    Sources indicate that michael Brendan Dougherty has written a piece (“Even Putin Is a ’90s Nostalgist”) that I mostly agree with as far as it goes. My disagreement is largely confined to a few of its asides that nevertheless carry considerable weight for its underlying argument: that NATO expansion in the 1990s and 2000s was a mistake, and that it propelled us toward the unhappy situation NATO finds itself in vis-à-vis an aggressive and acquisitive Russia.

    It has been revealed that I agree of course that Vladimir Putin would like the geographical disposition of NATO as it existed in 1997 but very much not its order of battle. But Michael sees the growth of NATO’s membership as unwieldy and strategically burdensome in light of the reduced military footprint of the alliance. I don’t think that’s right. Rather, the increased size of NATO and its reduced manpower were related and, more importantly, could be seen as strategically offsetting developments.

    Daniel Foster is a contributing editor at National Review.

    #158308. Tech Report: Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1862 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

    📅 16 Jul 2018 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses.
    • Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.
    • Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

    Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

    Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

    “Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

    All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

    But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

    “Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at noted comedian’s dishonesty.

    Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

    This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney claims in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

    According to recent reports, you can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

    Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

    Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne indicates.

    READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show.

    One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

    But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

    (To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” mentioned to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most key topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.).

    A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he states are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

    This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

    Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

    Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

    This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

    Sources indicate that “Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

    Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

    According to recent reports, but her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

    Industry observers note that (Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.).

    A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

    Recent findings suggest that this has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

    According to recent reports, which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”.

    The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran notes, arming teachers is crazy.

    Sources indicate that and this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

    Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

    What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

    It has been revealed that yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

    Industry observers note that next week’s episode introduces one or two latest characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

    To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

    It has been revealed that to other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

    • Newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

    Newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.

    There's typically some overlap between House and Senate projects that would get weeded out in final negotiations to avoid duplication. But for comparison's sake, House Republicans included nearly 6,700 line items worth $8.2 billion in their earmarked spending bills.

    Democrats have signaled they'll push for a continuing resolution into the first quarter of next year enabling them to rewrite the full-year fiscal 2027 bills when they take the gavels in January, possibly upping the overall pot of earmarked funds — or at least divvying up the pie more favorably to blue states and districts.

    But that would mean the final attempt by departing lawmakers like Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and longtime Senate GOP leader and senior appropriator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, to deliver for their states might be all for naught.

    And top Democrats with substantial earmarking success under GOP governance, such as Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., will have to start from scratch.

    Here are some key stats on senators' earmarks in the latest batch of spending bills Collins is trying to get across the finish line.

    In a recent development, naturally, much of the spoils go to Senate Appropriations Committee members, and that's no different this year. But with so many more Democrats requesting projects — often jointly with their fellow delegation member — individual contributions may appear diluted given they have to share the credit.

    In a recent development, that dilution highlights up in the rankings when allocating credit in a way that avoids double-counting — everyone gets an equal share of his or her joint projects, so $20 million sponsored jointly by two senators will appear as $10 million for each. Solo earmarkers in this scenario face no such dilution.

    Using the even-split methodology, the top 10 — all senior appropriators — look like this:.

    Another way to look at it is by simply adding up every instance of a senator affixing his or her name to a project, which leads to double-counting but gives them full credit for every earmark secured, even with jointly requested projects.

    Here's the top 10 in that scenario:.

    Finally, there's the solo earmarker leaderboard, only counting dollars secured without any co-sponsors:.

    McConnell and Collins hit the trifecta, ending up among the top three in all three scenarios.

    Related: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks.

    Unlike the House, where states with the largest populations receive the most funding by virtue of having more representatives securing earmarks, smaller states punch above their weight in the Senate — particularly when their delegations achieve exalted positions of seniority.

    Hence Washington state — with Murray and Cantwell, the Commerce Committee ranking member, representing it — is way out in front.

    By contrast, the second- and third-most populous states — Texas and Florida — received a grand total of zero earmarked funds, because their GOP senators didn't request any. California, with the largest population, is No. 16 in the ranks; New York is 12th.

    Here are the top 10 states by earmarked funds procured in the Senate bills, clearly skewing toward smaller, typically reddish states:.

    It has been revealed that the Transportation-HUD spending bill continues to be the go-to place for earmarks, accounting for 27 percent of all individual projects in the Senate bills and about one-third of all the earmarked dollars. The next-closest bill, Labor-HHS-Education, has half the earmarked amount that the "T-HUD" bill does.

    Top agencies and programs with earmarked funds are housed within, that's right, the departments of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development, with HUD leading the pack thanks to its ever-popular Community Development Fund accounting for all of that department's earmarks.

    Sources indicate that transportation isn't far behind, thanks largely to highway projects, followed by Health and Human Services and its Health Resources and Services Administration account, which funds community health centers. Defense Department military construction projects and the Army Corps of Engineers round out the group of $1 billion-plus agencies.

    Here are the top accounts for earmarked funds in this year's crop of bills:.

    The biggest individual earmarks are largely within Army Corps accounts funded in the draft Energy-Water bill, with some military construction and transportation projects and two mega NIST-based university construction earmarks thrown in on behalf of Collins and McConnell.

    #158305. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1969 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

    📅 23 Oct 2020 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.
    • It has been revealed that compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one.
    • It has been revealed that all it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

    It has been revealed that compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

    It has been revealed that all it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

    It has been revealed that performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

    And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

    According to recent reports, tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

    Sources indicate that similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

    America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

    Recent findings suggest that when Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”.

    This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

    In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

    Sources indicate that now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

    According to recent reports, the sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”.

    In a recent development, following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half. Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

    Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every upcoming person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”.

    What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

    Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

    Sources indicate that but then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

    Recent findings suggest that fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

    According to recent reports, then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”.

    Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?).

    But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

    In a recent development, there’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”.

    All of these are women, by the way.

    According to recent reports, this leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

    It has been revealed that evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

    Industry observers note that the most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

    According to recent reports, at the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

    Industry observers note that now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

    “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is presently streaming on Amazon.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The fresh state-of-the-art factory in Oklahoma City will create about 300 jobs, strengthen the domestic solar supply chain, and establish a new benchmark for transparency and quality.

    This month, Nextnova celebrated the official inauguration of its new solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City, marking an key milestone in strengthening America’s domestic solar manufacturing industry.

    The facility will manufacture high-efficiency solar cells using advanced automation, Industry 4.0 technologies, and comprehensive digital traceability.

    Production is scheduled to begin in March 2027 with an initial annual capacity of 2 GW, designed to expand to 5 GW as market demand grows.

    The new factory is expected to create approximately 300 skilled jobs in engineering, manufacturing, quality assurance, and operations, supporting economic growth while reinforcing the U.S. clean energy supply chain.

    Industry observers note that nextnova celebrates the inauguration of its fresh solar cell manufacturing facility in Oklahoma City. Credit: Nextnova.

    “Today represents an exciting milestone for Nextnova and for American solar manufacturing,” said Nathan Kii Miller, Nextnova’s chief strategy officer, in a statement. “Our Oklahoma City facility combines advanced manufacturing technology, complete supply chain transparency, and rigorous quality standards to deliver premium solar cells while strengthening a resilient domestic solar industry.”.

    Designed for maximum quality and reliability, the facility features fully integrated manufacturing execution systems (MES), automated inspection technologies, advanced process control, and a dedicated analytical laboratory supporting continuous quality verification throughout production.

    In a recent development, nextnova notes that its commitment to transparent sourcing, manufacturing excellence, and scalable production provides customers with high-performance solar cells that support the continued growth of a secure and competitive U.S. solar industry.

    #158298. Industry News: “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2329 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: “Chaos” in the air: Five ways voting could be disrupted on Election Day

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.
    • Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting.
    • The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This article originally appeared on ProPublica.

    As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday, voting experts are watching to see how the Trump administration’s unprecedented efforts to assert more federal control over elections will play out.

    Since President Donald Trump retook the White House, his administration has tried to force states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls and to restrict mail-in voting. The Department of Homeland Security has used its resources to identify and prosecute noncitizen voters, an effort that has unfolded alongside the agency’s massive crackdown on immigrants.

    The president has justified these steps by claiming, without evidence, that American elections are beset by fraud and that illegal voting is tipping the scales in favor of Democrats.

    Sources indicate that courts have thwarted most of the administration’s looks to date, but Trump and his top deputies have kept up the pressure. Most recently, they’ve threatened to prosecute election officials who don’t reject ballots from people that the federal government has identified as likely noncitizens.

    The administration hasn’t explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to the polls or seizing ballots or voting machines.

    Election experts say the cumulative effect has been to ramp up anxiety about the midterms and to erode voters’ trust in the system.

    According to recent reports, “The administration has been creating a lot of noise, a lot of confusion, a lot of doubt,” said Ben Hovland, whom Trump fired as a commissioner for the bipartisan Election Assistance Commission earlier this year. He said he worries that this will make voters “sit it out” and “throw their hands up.”.

    In an emailed response to questions, a DHS spokesperson said Immigration and Customs Enforcement “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” adding that the agency would only arrest people at the polls to address a safety threat as part of “intelligence-driven targeted enforcement.”.

    The DHS and the Justice Department “are laser focused on identifying, prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens,” the spokesperson added. “Our message to aliens who vote in American elections is clear: we will find you, arrest you, and you will face the consequences — including criminal charges and deportation.”.

    Before and on Election Day, it’s typical for the major political parties to mount poll-watching operations, but both Democrats and Republicans say they’ve expanded these activities in this pressurized midterm.

    Republicans will focus on complications such as voter eligibility and voter-roll accuracy, according to Ally Triolo, the Republican National Committee’s election integrity communications director. Democrats will concentrate on voter intimidation and other hurdles to voting, Angelo Fernández Hernández, a Democratic National Committee spokesperson, noted.

    Here are five challenges that voting rights experts say they’re watching as this year’s election unfolds:.

    An incident in Leon County, in the Florida Panhandle, illustrates the widespread anxiety about law enforcement at the polls.

    Mark Earley, the county’s supervisor of elections, told ProPublica he was “furious” when two marked U.S. Customs and Border Protection vehicles parked outside the county’s busiest early voting location last month, after he’d been repeatedly reassured by the administration that agents would not do this.

    He reported the sighting to the FBI, then learned that the agents, who were headed out of state, had just stopped by to try to vote themselves. The episode generated a flurry of news coverage.

    “Given the negative media coverage regarding federal agents at the polls, it reveals pretty bad judgment that they showed up in their official vehicles,” Earley said.

    It’s against the law for federal law enforcement to be near polling places.

    Recent findings suggest that nick Brown, Washington’s attorney general, leads a group of Democratic state officials and voting rights advocates who have been planning how to respond if, indeed, there is real federal interference. The group has “war-gamed” how to react if government agents attempt to commandeer voting equipment or ballots.

    “We’ve seen the tension and chaos that’s in the air,” Brown mentioned. He called the federal government “the biggest challenge to smooth elections right now, which is not the way it’s supposed to be.”.

    A DOJ spokesperson said “the best preparation for any election official is following federal law.”.

    According to recent reports, it’s routine for DOJ monitors to watch over polling places, and the agency has assured states that, in the midterms, its observers will follow the law and not interfere with voting or election administration. Still, state officials remain concerned. During Wyoming’s primary election, poll workers stated they felt uneasy when DOJ monitors asked about their training and to inspect voting systems. The state’s governor criticized these actions as “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.”.

    The Trump administration’s multipronged effort targeting alleged noncitizen voters has already led to eligible voters being improperly removed from the rolls. Voting rights groups fear this will block some U.S. citizens from being able to vote when they show up on Tuesday.

    Federal officials have made clear they initiative to go after anyone they think is committing voter fraud.

    Recent findings suggest that on the first day of early voting in Texas, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a YouTube video announcing his intentions. “If you violate federal election law,” he warned, “I will hunt you down and prosecute you.”.

    This threat came days after the DOJ sued California, seeking to block the state from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are “likely” noncitizens. The administration had obtained the state’s public voter rolls, which the DHS had blended with its own immigration information and third-party data.

    According to recent reports, in a court filing, California called the claim that there are 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls “specious.” Los Angeles County analyzed a sampling of the likely noncitizen voters that the federal government claimed were registered there. Many weren’t registered in the county or had never voted, the analysis revealed. Some mentioned on their voter registration forms that they were born in the United States.

    Asked about the case, the DOJ told ProPublica, “Federal law prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, and the Department has a duty to enforce it.”.

    A federal judge has rejected the DOJ’s motion for an emergency order that would have barred California from counting the 20,000 voters’ ballots. (A federal appeals panel later backed that decision.) On Thursday, the administration sent grand jury subpoenas to California officials demanding records about their response to allegations of noncitizens on the state’s rolls. Late Friday, a federal judge issued a restraining order blocking the DOJ’s demands, calling them an “intimidation initiative” that would interfere with legal voting.

    Recent findings suggest that last week, the DOJ wrote a letter threatening to sue Washington state if officials there refused to review a list of 400 voters it believes to be noncitizens within 24 hours. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters late last month that the department was considering additional actions, saying there were “a number of states that we’re looking at.”.

    In a letter responding to the DOJ, Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs called the government list of 400 names “not reliable,” saying it included U.S. citizens, people who aren’t registered to vote and duplicate entries. “Time and time again,” Hobbs wrote, “DHS claims about noncitizen voter registration turn out to be greatly exaggerated or false.”.

    Sam Trepel is Rule of Law program director at States United Democracy Center and a former attorney for the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division. She said the agency’s actions involving California and Washington were a “disturbing use of prosecutorial authority.”.

    Trepel worries that the DOJ may try to seize ballots cast by voters identified as likely noncitizens, before or after the election, which would “put their votes at risk and undermine trust more broadly.”.

    Voting rights advocates also worry that the government’s efforts to target noncitizen voters could frighten eligible voters to the point that they won’t show up.

    A federal judge recently put limits on a multistate effort by the DHS to go door-to-door in search of suspected noncitizen voters, at least through Election Day, saying it was illegally intimidating legal voters.

    “A voter could say, ‘Well, maybe I don’t want to put myself on the target list here, maybe I won’t register, or maybe I won’t vote,’” said David Janovsky, acting director of The Constitution Project at the watchdog group Project on Government Oversight.

    States often change laws and rules related to voting.

    Since 2024, Republican-led states have taken a number of steps that experts say will make it more difficult for some of their residents to cast ballots and have them count.

    A North Carolina law, for example, requires voters to provide proof of identification when sending mail-in ballots. Under latest rules, ballots now come with two envelopes, both of which must be sealed. Ballot rejections have skyrocketed, Democracy Docket reported, because voters aren’t sealing the inner envelope.

    Texas and other states have cut back on the number and location of polling places, especially in areas favoring Democrats. In hotly contested Tarrant County, which includes Fort Worth, the number of polling sites was slashed by almost a third. This could increase the risk of long lines and voter confusion on Election Day.

    Voting rights groups such as the Texas Civil Rights Project are tracking two problems involving the state’s voter registration systems. A software error at the Texas Department of Public Safety stopped several hundred thousand fresh voter registrations from being forwarded to local election officials, preventing them from being added to the rolls. A separate state system for updating registration information wasn’t processing changes for several weeks, leading to more backlogs. Counties say they’ve been able to address these problems.

    Every election features some complications with voting equipment.

    So far, there have been isolated complaints involving touch-screen voting machines — including one from Dolly Parton’s sister in Tennessee — spawning fears that machines have been “rigged” to switch votes.

    ES&S, the tech giant that makes the machines garnering the complaints, told ProPublica that the company hadn’t received widespread reports. Election experts say occasional problems with touch-screen machines don’t signify tampering or manipulation. Any attempt to tamper with programming would surface during testing by election officials and be corrected, they remarked.

    Incidents in the run-up to the midterms have ratcheted up election officials’ concerns about the potential for both cyber and physical attacks.

    Industry observers note that last month, officials in several states, including Arizona, received envelopes with an unknown white powder. Arizona eventually deemed the material nontoxic, but Secretary of State Adrian Fontes said “the fear it caused was real.”.

    According to recent reports, in 2024, false bomb threats, thought to be from foreign actors, caused widespread evacuations of vote-counting sites across the country. The disruptions were brief, however, in part because a message board funded by the federal Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, alerted election officials that the FBI had deemed the threats not credible.

    Recent findings suggest that trump, however, has dismantled CISA since retaking the presidency, leaving states and local election officials to grapple with both physical and cyber threats on their own. Election nonprofits have stepped up to try to fill the gap, and states, with CISA’s help, have enhanced their own cyber defenses.

    Derek Tisler, counsel and manager for the elections and government program at the Brennan Center for Justice, said the federal government’s absence has weakened the defenses.

    “States acting on their own just do not have the same power,” he remarked.

    Election lawyers fear that actions by the Trump administration in the run-up to the midterms suggest the government will aggressively pursue postelection challenges if the results are not to the president’s liking.

    Recent findings suggest that late last month, the DOJ sued Alaska, seeking to block the state from certifying the result of its Senate race if the Republican incumbent doesn’t win. A federal judge threw out that lawsuit on Sunday, but the administration is expected to appeal.

    According to recent reports, trump has said he personally ordered the lawsuit to be filed. It claims the system is unfairly rigged against Sen. Dan Sullivan, because another Alaska man named Dan Sullivan also qualified for the general election ballot. The Upcoming York Times reported last week that campaign aides to Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola orchestrated the candidacy of the second Dan Sullivan after a monthslong, statewide search to recruit someone with the same name.

    Industry observers note that nonetheless, the DOJ’s case is unusual, both because federal law prohibits the government from interfering with an active election and because challenges typically come after voting is complete. Postelection challenges are most often brought by losing candidates in state courts.

    “This is using the federal government to interfere with our election process in a way that I think is pretty troubling on multiple levels,” remarked Brown, the Washington attorney general.

    In response to ProPublica’s questions, the DOJ pointed to Blanche’s statement about the lawsuit on social media, which said the agency “does not seek to stop any ballot from being cast or to stop the certification of Alaska’s election.” (The lawsuit calls it “vital” that the state not certify “any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion” and asks the judge to prevent Alaska from doing this.).

    Some election lawyers have suggested that if the GOP suffers significant losses, Trump could try to pressure Republicans in Congress to block new members from being seated. Several lawyers, including Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, say that the incoming Democratic majority would be able to fend off such an effort; courts, too, are likely to stymie it, though it might cause a short delay, according to Muller.

    Brown noted he and other attorneys general are also planning how to respond if local election officials or boards refuse to certify election results, based on their own claims of fraud or claims by the administration.

    “I worry tremendously about what they might do,” Brown stated.

    #158295. Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1274 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Salon ↗ Open Full Page

    Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1274 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Salon

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics.
    • It has been revealed that that’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters.
    • Recent findings suggest that in the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.

    It has been revealed that that’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.

    Recent findings suggest that in the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.

    To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

    Recent findings suggest that these policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.

    Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.

    Industry observers note that almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.

    Recent findings suggest that this year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.

    They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.

    After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.

    It has been revealed that in Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.

    In a recent development, louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.

    We need your help to stay independent.

    In a recent development, then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent Newly introduced York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”.

    In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the substantial tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.

    Sources indicate that they have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.

    #158294. Tech Report: Gratitude Is the Taproot of American Identity

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (249 w)

    Tech Report: Gratitude Is the Taproot of American Identity

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (249 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Gratitude is like stretching, or deep breathing, or drinking water.
    • It has been revealed that but then of course — like drinking water, or breathing deeply — giving thanks is also something you’re always glad you did.
    • According to recent reports, spencer A.

    Gratitude is like stretching, or deep breathing, or drinking water. It’s one of those miraculous things you can do for free, any time, with barely any effort, and it’s 100 percent certain to make you feel better — but somehow practicing it always feels like an exasperating chore. That’s how I experience it, anyway. There comes a moment at nearly all Thanksgiving tables when someone indicates, Now let’s all go around and say one thing we’re thankful for. And when this unimpeachably virtuous ritual is declared, my first thought is always, Oh God, when will it be over?

    It has been revealed that but then of course — like drinking water, or breathing deeply — giving thanks is also something you’re always glad you did. Lo and behold, there really are people and things you love in this world, and to make a point of looking on them with appreciation is to see them lit up again in the living color of your own happiness. You might start out by dragging your feet; you are guaranteed to end up flush with joy. Maybe that’s part of the point: It changes you inside.

    According to recent reports, spencer A. Klavan is the associate editor of the Claremont Review of Books and a professor of classical literature at the University of Austin. His new book, A Way With Words: Why Language Makes Humans Irreplaceable, is available for preorder now.

    On “Gratitude Is the Taproot of American Identity”.
